_hand_authored: Hand-mapped against public/hero/base-photo.png. UNLIKE hero-scene.json (generated by scripts/render-base-scene.mjs from a real camera) this plate is an AI-generated photograph with no camera to project from, so every number here was measured off the image with scripts/hero-grid.mjs and checked against a real composite via /hero-check + scripts/hero-shot.mjs. Edit it by hand, re-shoot, and look at the result — several of these corners were wrong by 2-4% on the first pass and only the composite showed it.
_geometry_note: Coordinates are PERCENTAGES of the plate (0-100), x rightward, y downward. lib/hero-regions.ts divides by 100 to reach the 0-1 fractions the compositor works in. Percentages because that is the unit the mapping grid prints, and hand-editing 41.4 is less error-prone than 0.414. Quads are topLeft, topRight, bottomRight, bottomLeft in TEXTURE order (corner i of the quad is corner i of the texture).

faces._plate2_perspective: THE SOLVE FOR THIS PLATE, in one place, because every wall number below is derived from it rather than eyeballed. Measured with a bilinear luminance probe, not read off a zoom. (1) BACK WALL CEILING LINE: strongest downward-brightening gradient in 13 columns from x=23.5 to 43, least squares y = 4.9885 + 0.11627x, max residual 0.12% — this plate's ceiling is genuinely straight, unlike the previous one's. (2) BACK WALL PAN LINE: darkest row per column, x=27..43.5, y = 89.0014 - 0.097911x, residuals under one pixel. (3) HORIZON is where those two meet: y = 50.60, vanishing point x = 392.2. The plate is 336px tall so its centre row is y=50.0 — the camera is level and its principal point is the frame centre, which is the assumption everything else leans on, and it falls out of the measurement rather than being imposed on it. (4) LEFT RETURN CEILING LINE: the diagonal running up and left out of the top of the frame, 10 columns x=19.4..22.1, slope 2.36552, max residual 0.18. It meets the horizon at x=40.39, so VP2 = (40.39, 50.60). (5) FOCAL LENGTH from those two vanishing points being perpendicular about the principal point: f^2 = (392.2-50)(50-40.39), so f = 56.7% of plate width, a horizontal field of 82.8deg. Wide, but that is what an interior plate looks like. (6) CAMERA HEIGHT above the pan, anchored on the back wall being 60in: project both of its pan corners onto the ground plane and set their separation to 60in, giving D = 42.15in. (7) VERTICAL MODEL, which is all the compositor actually needs: y = 50.60 + (y_pan - 50.60) * (1 - h/42.15) for a height h above the pan, on any plane, applied to that plane's own pan line. CONSISTENCY TEST: the ceiling solves to h/D = 2.18751 at the interior corner and 2.18753 at the right edge — two independently measured lines agreeing to five figures, which is not something that happens by accident. Ceiling height 92.2in above the pan.
faces._plate2_span_assignment: WHICH SPAN IS 60in AND WHICH IS 32in, settled by geometry rather than assumed. The alcove has three vertical boundaries: the room corner at x=15.05, the interior corner at x=22.2 and the right edge at x=44.49, so the candidates are 22.2->44.49 (22.29% of plate width) and 15.05->22.2 (7.15%). ASSIGNMENT A, back wall = the wide span: 0.371%/in against the return's 0.225%/in, the return foreshortened to 61%, an ordinary oblique view. ASSIGNMENT B, back wall = the narrow span: the return would be foreshortened to 17% of the back wall, a 10deg grazing angle, which contradicts its ceiling line falling at 2.37%y per %x — that is a steep recession, not a grazing one. B also fails outright on height: the back wall measures 79.2% of plate height pan-to-ceiling against 22.29% of plate width, a ratio of 1.53 once the 2.333 aspect is taken out, so a 32in-wide back wall would stand 48in tall. A gives 92in. A WINS. THE 32in IS THEN CONFIRMED THREE TIMES OVER, none of them the anchor: (i) the door's bottom rail at (38, 93.45) projects to 31.2in in front of the back wall; (ii) the pan's own front threshold projects to a depth of 31.4in; (iii) the pan is therefore 60 x 31.4in, which is a catalogue 60x32 base. The wall plane carries on PAST the enclosure to the room corner at 15.05, and that extra span is room, not shower — which is why showerWallLeft stops at the door post.
faces._alcove_corners: All four vertical boundaries found by sub-pixel darkest-column search, sampled at 13-17 heights each and reported with their spread, because a boundary that moves between samples is a shading contour and not a corner. INTERIOR CORNER: x=22.19 to 22.32 over y=4..62, a spread of 0.13%, so the whole line lives inside one pixel. Least squares gives 22.22 at the ceiling drifting to 22.34 at the pan — a lean of 0.12% over the wall's height, under a pixel, honoured only because it keeps the seam on the plate's own dark column at every height. Cross-check: the two ceiling lines intersect at x=22.09, 0.13% from the luminance corner. ALCOVE RIGHT EDGE: 44.486-44.500 at every height from y=26 to 82, dead vertical, no drift at all. (Rows y=58 and 62 read 44.27 and are excluded — that is the door handle, luminance 24 against the edge's 140.) ROOM CORNER, outside the enclosure: a thin dark line at 15.04-15.07 from y=2 to 62, also dead vertical. DOOR POST: left edge 15.82-15.94, right edge 16.44-16.46, core luminance 7-12. A vertical world line projects vertical only under a camera with no roll, and all four of these are vertical — the fourth independent confirmation of the solve above. WHAT THE PREVIOUS PASS GOT WRONG: it recorded the interior corner at x=31.2. There is a narrow dark line there, 1% wide with matched shoulders, constant at every height — but it is the sliding door's leading glass edge, not a corner. The real corner is 9% further left, and the broad luminance fall from x=18 to 22.5 that surrounds it (187 down to 91 at y=7) is the return raking away from the light, exactly the signature the previous plate had at its own corner.
faces._alcove_scale: Why these are separate planes rather than one warped sheet. Back wall 60in over 22.29% of plate width, left return 40in over 6.10%: 0.371%/in against 0.152%/in, so the return is foreshortened to 41% of the back wall's scale and one quad spanning both could not tile a 24in panel correctly on either. At 24in panels the back wall is 2.5 panels, giving joints at 24in and 48in from the corner; the return is 1-2/3 panels, giving one joint at 24in from the corner. The return's quad is ordered CORNER-FIRST — topLeft is the interior corner, not the outer edge — so tiling starts at the corner, a full panel terminates there, and the offcut falls at the outer end where the door post covers it. That is how the kit installs.
faces._panel_top_derivation: THE PANEL TOP FOLLOWS THE CEILING, at a fixed 0.30% clearance below the measured line, and that is a decision the numbers forced. 94.5in above the pan projects to y=5.61 at the interior corner and y=8.31 at the right edge; the ceiling there is 7.57 and 10.16. So a full-height panel overshoots this plate's alcove by 1.96% and 1.86% of plate height respectively — it would end ABOVE the ceiling. The alcove is 92.2in tall, so the honest install cuts 2.7in off a 94.5in panel, and the rendered field is 91.8in with the cut edge at the ceiling. This is the outcome the previous plate made impossible (there the panel fell short and stranded a band of bare wall), and it needs no departure from scale: heightIn is 91.8 on both planes and the vertical model reproduces it at the corner (91.87in), the right edge (91.83in) and the return's outer end (91.58in), all within a quarter inch. The 0.30% clearance is there so antialiasing on the top line cannot poke above the ceiling; at this plate's resolution it is one pixel. All plane tops meet at the shared corner vertex (22.20, 7.87) — one point, no step.
faces._left_return_extent: showerWallLeft runs from the interior corner OUT TO THE DOOR POST at x=16.10, not to the room corner at 15.05. The post occupies 15.85-16.44, so terminating the plane at 16.10 puts the panel's outer edge underneath it: the post hides the termination and no sliver of bare plate can open beside it. Stopping at the honest 32in instead would land at x=17.42 and leave a full 1% of plate width of untinted wall standing between the panel and the post, which reads as a gap. So the plane spans 40in of this plate's 44in-deep wall — the same trade already made on panel height, for the same reason, and widthIn says 40 so the 24in joint still lands at true scale. ITS TOP RUNS OFF THE FRAME, and this time that is measured rather than worked around: the return's ceiling line has a real fitted slope of 2.366 and crosses y=0 at x=18.87. The previous plate used y=-17 because no ceiling could be found above the return at all; here the ceiling is found, fitted to 0.18% residuals, and simply leaves the top of a 2.33:1 crop. paintPanelTopEdge now clips the edge at the frame instead of dropping the whole segment, so the part still in shot is drawn as a product edge and the join at the corner reads.
faces._right_return_dropped: THERE IS NO THIRD WALL ON THIS PLATE, and the strip that looks like one is measured out rather than argued away. Profiles across x=43.8..47.0 at nine heights show the back wall's tone running flat to a shallow minimum at x=44.50, then a BRIGHT band rising to a peak of 180 at x=45.14 (against the back wall's 150 in the same row), then a hard dark line at x=45.92 that does not move by more than 0.02% between y=6 and y=84, then the vanity wall. That band is the brightest thing anywhere in the alcove, so it is lit from the vanity side, not from inside the shower. GEOMETRY AGREES: the partition's shower-facing plane sits at world X = -0.38 to -0.26 in camera-height units, entirely to the LEFT of the camera axis, while its outward normal points further left still — the camera is on its back side and that face cannot be visible at all. Whatever the band is (the partition's corner radius catching light, or the slider's right jamb), it is not shower interior, and multiplying a dark panel colour over 0.9% of the plate's brightest highlight would draw a black stripe down the edge of the shower. So wallColors[2] is a no-op on the photo plate: PHOTO_FACES still lists showerWallRight, this key is simply absent, the region resolves to zero faces and the compositor's own faces.length guard skips it. The Three.js plate is untouched and still paints all three.
faces._floor_perimeter: PAN OUTLINE, corrected in this pass. It is not the parallelogram the previous pass authored. The pan's back-left corner is the INTERIOR CORNER (22.34, 86.81), not x=17: left of the corner there is no back wall for the pan to meet, only the return, and the pan's left edge runs from that corner down and toward the camera along the return's own base line. FRONT THRESHOLD: measured at x=26 and x=30, the two columns the sliding door does not cover — the pan floor ends at y=94.75 and 94.45 respectively, and the line through them toward the back wall's vanishing point is y = 98.082 - 0.12106x. The previous quad ran (17,99.30)->(44.8,94.55), a slope of -0.171, which put the front edge 2.63% of plate height too low at x=30 and painted pan across the curb and onto the room floor. For x>32 the threshold is hidden under the door's bottom rail (a black bar falling from y=93.85 at x=34 to 92.65 at x=44), so it is projected rather than measured there, which is why the perspective solve had to come first. CORNERS: back-left (22.34, 86.81), back-right (44.49, 84.65), front-right (45.45, 92.58) where the front line meets the partition's base, front-left (17.80, 95.93) where it meets the return's base — behind the plant, so projected. The pan then measures 60 x 31.4in, i.e. a 60x32 base, and heightIn is corrected from 34 to 32.
faces._counter_ends: Left end re-measured this pass at three rows by sub-pixel step search: the wall-to-counter step sits at x=49.15 on the counter surface (y=56.5), 49.15 in the splash band (53.5) and 49.25 at the nosing (57.5). The counter's own left end is a vertical plane whose top edge is further from the camera, so that 0.1% lean is real and the quads now carry it. Right end unchanged at 77.3. The previous 47.0-71.0 reading in this note was the OLD plate and is gone.
faces._backsplash_note: A band of the same material standing on the counter's back edge and running up the wall. Height is derived, not measured off the plate — the plate has no splash to measure. The vanity reads 36in to the counter top over 33% of image height at this depth, i.e. 0.917% per inch, so a 4in splash is 3.7% and a 6in splash 5.5%; the compositor scales the band from the vanity's own backsplash selection.
faces._backsplash_right_end: The splash stops at x=65.7, NOT at the counter's right end at x=71.0. There is a wall corner at x=65.0 (y=5) leaning to 65.6 (y=48) — visible as a break in the ceiling line above and confirmed by the wall tone changing across it — and a splash runs along a wall, so it ends where the wall turns. The counter itself is unaffected and still runs the full 47.0 to 71.0. The consequence is deliberate and visible: roughly 5% of plate width of bare wall sits above the counter's right end.

_clip_note: Where a texture is ALLOWED to land, as against the quad which says how it warps. This plate has no rendered ID mask (the Three.js scene had one), so occlusion is hand-traced instead. First polygon of each list is the outer boundary; a polygon nested inside another punches a hole, via the even-odd fill rule. A HOLE MUST LIE ENTIRELY INSIDE ITS OUTER POLYGON — even-odd counts crossings, so any part of a hole that pokes out the other side flips back to filled and paints where nothing should. That is why the plant cut-out below stops just short of the wall's bottom edge instead of running past it. Traced deliberately tight: under-covering leaves a sliver of plate showing, which reads as shadow; over-covering smears material across a plant or a toilet, which reads as broken.
_plant_note: The plant cut-out in backWall is the one place a polygon is the wrong tool. A fern has no outline, so this is a compromise between two visible failures: too tight and wall material paints stripes across the leaves, too loose and a grey wedge of bare plate opens up beside them. It is tuned to hug the dense core and let the sparse outer fronds take a little bleed, because bleed on a few leaf tips reads as shadow while the grey wedge reads as a hole. A per-pixel mask keyed off the foliage's green would beat this outright and is the obvious next step if it ever needs to be better.
_clip_simplification: These used to carry notches cut around the plants, the toilet and the plant pots. They don't any more: public/hero/base-photo-occlusion.png restores every foreground object over the finished composite in one pass, so a clip only has to describe the SURFACE now, not what happens to be standing on it. Where a boundary still bends, it is following real geometry — the vanity toe kick, the partition base, the shower curb — not an obstacle.
_seams_note: Ambient occlusion the compositor paints along a corner AFTER the materials land. The plate already carries its own corner darkening and multiply passes it straight through, so these are deliberately WEAKER than what is measured. MEASURED ON THIS PLATE, at y=30: the interior corner reads 150.2 at its darkest column against a smooth interpolation of its immediate neighbours at ~154, so the LOCAL crease is only about 4 units, 3% — the big fall from 178 at x=20 is the return's own shading, which multiply already carries. The right edge reads 147 against shoulders of 150 and 154, also about 4 units but over 0.3% of width rather than 3%. Strengths below are set near those measurements rather than imported from the previous plate, whose corner was three times deeper. `from`/`to` are the corner's endpoints and `halfWidthPct` the fade distance either side, both in plate percent. NOTE: only alcoveInterior, alcoveRight and partitionFloor are painted by the compositor; the vanity and pan entries are kept as the measurement record.

alcoveInterior._measured: Soft. Darkest column 22.19-22.32 at every height. TWO components: a narrow crease about 4 units deep on a 154 shoulder, and the broad V of the return raking away from the light, 178 at x=20 down to 150 at 22.5. Multiply carries most of the broad one through; strength is set between the two because at the narrow crease's own value the corner did not read once a slat texture flattened it.

alcoveRight._measured: Hard and narrow. Darkest column 44.486-44.500 at every height, depth ~4 units over 0.3%.

panWallLeft._measured: Pan meeting the back wall, along the fitted junction y = 89.0014 - 0.097911x.

vanityLeft._measured: Hard dark line at x=49.5 between wall and cabinet face.

vanityRight._measured: Cabinet right edge at x=77.45, dark line to 77.6.

vanityToe._measured: Toe line re-measured this pass at four columns: 87.4 at x=52, 86.8 at 58, 86.3 at 64, 85.6 at 70 — slope -0.100, the same slope as the pan's back edge, which is what two horizontal floor lines parallel to the back wall must share.

_fixture_note: Boxes around the plate's baked-in matte-black hardware, for recolouring it to the dealer's selected finish. Given as [x, y, w, h] in plate percentages, GROUPED: a group is one finish choice, and it carries a list of boxes because the sliding door's hardware is one choice spread over nine separate pieces of metal. The tint only touches pixels below a luminosity cutoff of 112, so wall, counter and cast shadow inside a box are left alone — which is what makes a slightly generous box safe. It is NOT safe when something else dark falls inside, and on this plate that is the real constraint: the head, the track and the valve are close enough that one loose box catches its neighbour. Every number below was found by counting sub-cutoff pixels per column and per row across a search window, then reading the clusters off, not by eye.
_fixture_faucet_note: The lavatory faucet is two boxes, not one, because a full-width box spanning the spout's height also spans the hard shadow line under the mirror frame at y=48.5 — 44 of 49 pixels across that row sit below the cutoff, so the whole line recoloured and the vanity grew a gold stripe above the tap. The spout gets its own narrow box through that band; the wide box picks up below it, where the handles are and the mirror's shadow is not.
_fixture_head_note: The back-wall head region is GONE. The plate's baked-in head and its cast shadow are now painted out by plateRepairs before anything composites, and a modelled head is drawn on the LEFT return instead — see modeledHead. Leaving a tint box on the back wall would recolour a fixture that is no longer there.
_anchor_note: The anchors below are used ONLY by the Three.js fallback plate and are stale against this photo plate; the photo plate recolours the baked-in fixtures above instead of pinning product photographs. They are kept because that fallback still pins photos, and because the measurements are the record of where the plate's fixtures actually are. The plate has matte-black fixtures baked in. A product photo is pinned OVER each one and has to cover it outright, because multiply can darken the black blob but can never erase it. unitPerIn is therefore sized from the measured pixel footprint of the baked-in fixture, not from room geometry — this plate is generative and is not dimensionally consistent (solving its shower head and valve heights together puts the floor at 115% of frame).
_anchor_sizing: Solve unitPerIn = targetWidthFraction * plateAspect / (sizeIn * PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO * contentFraction), where plateAspect is 784/336 = 2.3333 and targetWidthFraction is the product's wanted width as a fraction of plate WIDTH. contentFraction is the share of the catalog frame the product actually fills, and it is the term that matters: scripts/measure-fixtures.mjs finds these three shots filling 94-100% of their frame, NOT the 1/1.5 that PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO assumes, so every overlay drew about 1.5x too large until this was measured rather than trusted. PHOTO_FRAME_RATIO is left at 1.5 because the Three.js plate's anchors were tuned around it and changing it would silently resize the fallback; it is divided back out here instead. Re-run measure-fixtures.mjs if the catalogue's crop ever changes. sizeIn is whatever the caller resolves from the component catalogue — 6in shower head, 6.5in trim, 8.9in faucet.

faucet._covers: baked-in x 54.9-60.0, y 47.9-55.5 (40 x 26 px). Drawn 7.0% of plate width.
faucet._y_note: Centred on 50.3 rather than on the fixture's own centre so the faucet STANDS on the counter. Its photo fills the frame's full width but only 63.5% of its height, centred, so the product's base falls 31.8% of the frame below the anchor — 5.2% of plate height at this scale. The counter's top edge under the faucet is y=55.5, hence 55.5 - 5.2.

showerTrim._covers: baked-in x 20.3-24.3, y 46.5-56.2 (31 x 33 px). Drawn 4.5% of plate width.

showerHead._covers: baked-in x 30.6-35.0, y 6.7-16.0 (35 x 31 px). Drawn 5.5% of plate width.

tubSpout._covers: nothing — this plate has a walk-in shower, no tub. Callers only pin a spout when the dealer picked a tub path, which this plate cannot depict; the anchor exists to satisfy the AnchorId union and puts the spout somewhere plausible rather than at 0,0.

_vanity_junction_note: Both cabinet ends measured by darkest-column search, and they are hard lines, not fades. LEFT: the reveal between the partition face and the cabinet side sits at x=46.94 and does not move between y=59 and y=86 — dead vertical — deepening from 47% to 88% below its shoulders as it descends into shadow. The profile at y=70 runs partition face 194 at x=46.5, then a genuine dark gap of 38-96 from 46.7 to 47.6, then cabinet 177 from 47.9. That gap is REAL geometry photographed in the plate, not a rendering artifact, so the cabinet region now stops at its true edge of 47.85 and the gap is left as plate. RIGHT: the cabinet ends at x=70.70 with its junction line at 70.75 (lum 31-34, depth ~0.70, constant y=62-74). The region previously stopped at 70.00, which left 0.7% of plate width of un-tinted cabinet standing between the composited colour and the wall — that is the gap the markup circled. Contact seams at both lines firm up the read after tinting; they are deliberately light because the plate's own junction shadows are already deep and multiply carries them through.
_plate_repairs_note: EMPTY. The old plate's head paint-out is obsolete — its box lands on bare wall in the new plate and would gouge a patch out of it. The new plate needs no repairs unless a survey finds a defect.
_modeled_head_note: RETIRED. This mechanism existed because the previous plate photographed its head on the wrong wall, so it had to be painted out by plateRepairs and redrawn. THIS plate photographs the head on the left return at a true 72in above the pan (solve it against _plate2_perspective: the arm's centreline at y=18.3 gives h/D = 1.7146, so h = 72.0in), which is a real fixture height and the right wall. So there is nothing to paint out and nothing to draw: the head is the showerHead group above and is recoloured like every other piece of metal. lib/hero-regions.ts sets modeledHead to null for the photo scene; the field, the type and drawModeledHead stay for the Three.js path.
_phase2_survey: PHASE 2 measurements, all zoom-verified on the NEW plate before use. PAN: back edge (24.5,87.8)->(44.5,84.5), slope -0.165/%x; front threshold, a hard dark line, (30,94.8)->(44.5,92.3), slope -0.172/%x; curb face runs about 2.3% below that. Left edge is behind the plant so it is extrapolated to x=17.0 along both lines — the polygon is the pan's TRUE outline, not what is unobscured. CABINET: left junction a hard dark line at x=49.5 with the face starting 50.0; right edge at x=77.3 with its own dark line to 77.6; top under the counter shadow at y=59.3; toe line (where the face ends and the recess begins) 87.3 at x=50 falling to 85.8 at x=70; floor begins y=90.0. COUNTER BAND splits in two and the earlier survey read them as one: the BACKSPLASH is the upper band, top (49.4,51.8)->(77.3,52.6), bottom 55.8->55.4; the COUNTER surface plus its nosing runs 55.8->58.2. There is also a RIGHT SIDE SPLASH, a narrow wood strip at x 77.3-78.1 from y 50.6 to 58.2, which the old plate did not have. PAN CORRECTION: the back-edge slope is -0.106/%x fitted across all four measured profile points, not the -0.165 first read off a zoom crop; that error put the top-left corner 1.25% too low and left a strip of untinted pan showing along the wall.
_phase2_deltas: Corrections found by zoom AFTER the regions first landed, logged because every pass so far has produced some. (1) Cabinet left edge 50.0 -> 49.6: the plate's cabinet stile catches light between the junction shadow at 49.3-49.5 and the face, and stopping at 50.0 left that 0.4% as an untinted sliver. (2) Side splash band 50.6-58.2 -> 52.6-55.4: authored from a first reading that made it stand 2% proud of the back splash and read as a tab; it is the same 4in element and meets the back splash on the shared line at x=77.3. (3) Not geometry: the fixtureRegions still hold OLD-plate boxes and were recolouring a patch of the new counter gold — gated off in the compositor until Phase 3 rebuilds them, same reasoning as the occlusion mask.
_fixture_measurements: WHAT THE PROBE FOUND, and what the banked Phase-1/2 numbers got wrong. SHOWER HEAD: dark mass x 19.13-23.09, y 17.26-23.70. The banked 17-27 x 14-23.6 was three separate things merged — the DOOR POST contributes 4-5 sub-cutoff pixels to every row it crosses (it is a full-height black column at x 15.94-16.33), and the TRACK contributes 25-97 pixels to rows 14.3-16.4. Neither belongs to the head. Nothing dark sits below the head: x 23-30, y 23-32 returns zero sub-cutoff pixels, so the head casts no shadow this tint could smear. VALVE: dark mass x 18.75-22.19, y 48.51-56.55, of which x 18.88-20.15 is the escutcheon (18-27px per column) and 20.28-22.07 the lever (3-8px). The banked 16-22 x 42-54 again included the post and started 6.5% too high. FAUCET: dark mass x 58.42-64.16, y 48.81-55.95. SCONCE: three sockets and the arm between them, x 56.25-66.71, y 6.85-12.50; the bulbs below are the brightest thing in the plate and the cutoff drops them without help. DOOR HARDWARE: post x 15.82-16.45 (solid core 15.94-16.33) running y 10.42-96.43; track rail measured at five spans, y 14.29-15.48 at x=17-20, 14.58-16.07 at 22-26, 15.48-16.67 at 30-34, 16.07-17.26 at 36-40, 16.37-17.86 at 41-44.8, i.e. a straight rail falling 0.0935%y per %x, carried as four stepped boxes rather than one 4%-tall box; hanger wheels x 32.4-33.16 and 43.11-43.49; handle a solid bar x 44.01-44.77, y 46.73-62.50; bottom rail y 92.56-94.35 across x 30.9-45.7.
_faucet_split_note: ONE BOX, NOT TWO — the opposite of what the previous plate needed, and measured rather than assumed. There IS a clean vertical break in the faucet's dark mass at x 60.08-60.84, where the minimum luminosity is 111 and no pixel falls under the cutoff, so the spout and the handle cluster genuinely do resolve separately. That is not why the old plate was split, though. It was split because a hard shadow line under the mirror ran THROUGH the box's y range and 44 of 49 pixels across that row sat below the cutoff, so the whole line recoloured. On this plate the two bands that would do that both sit OUTSIDE the faucet's own y range: the mirror frame's bottom shadow occupies y 47.02-48.51 (8-16 sub-cutoff pixels per row, minimum luminosity 72-95) and the counter/cabinet shadow y 58.63-58.93 (48-111 pixels). The faucet's own dark starts at y=48.81 with a minimum of 25. Starting the box at y=48.7 divides them cleanly, so a single box carries the whole fixture and the vertical gap inside it simply tints nothing.
_sconce_note: The vanity light USED to be excluded on the grounds that it is decor rather than something the dealer picks. That call is reversed here on instruction: it is now a tint group and follows the plumbing finish. The box covers the arm, the backplate and the three sockets, and stops at y=12.5 — the bulbs hang below that and are the brightest pixels anywhere in the plate, so the cutoff would drop them regardless; the box is kept off them anyway so the glow halo has no chance to fall under the cutoff at its edges.
_door_post_extent_note: The post's TINT box stops at y=65.5 although the post itself runs to 96.4, and that is a consequence of the compositing order rather than of the measurement. Occlusion restore runs BEFORE fixture tinting (it has to — see the compositor), so anything the mask puts back can be painted over by a tint box that overlaps it. Below y=65.5 the plant's foliage climbs across the post, and a tint box carried down through it would recolour leaves. Above 65.5 the post is clear of the plant. The mask restores the post over its full height, so under Matte Black it reads whole; under a light finish the covered lower third stays dark, which is where the leaves are anyway.
_fixture_deltas: Corrections found by rendering, because the first pass always leaves some. (1) TRACK END CAP untinted: the rail's fourth span and the right hanger both stopped at x=45.1-45.3, and the track's end stop runs to 45.75 — it stayed matte black against a gold rail. Both boxes now reach 45.85. That deliberately reaches 1.35% past the alcove's right edge at 44.49 and across the plate's BRIGHTEST vertical strip (the partition corner, luminosity 150-190 against the shower wall's 150), which is safe for exactly the reason the whole scheme is safe: the cutoff is 112 and the strip never goes near it. Verified in the harness row 9 — the handle recolours and the strip beside it does not. (2) DOOR POST tint capped at y=65.5, which is where the plant's first leaf crosses it. Rendered, the cut lands ON the leaf edge and reads as the post going behind the plant.
_door_glass_note: THE GLASS, and the evidence for where it is. Multiply carries the plate's glazing through darkly and drops it brightly, so with a dark panel selected the glazed half of the alcove came out identical to the unglazed half — the door simply vanished. The compositor now redraws the plate over these outlines in `screen`, which can only add light. TWO SHEETS, NOT ONE, and the profile says so at every height from y=22 to y=88 without varying: reading across x=29.4 to 32.2 there are TWO parallel dark minima, at x=30.31 and x=31.22, with a distinct plateau between them that is darker than the field on either side. That is a lap joint — one sheet's edge, the other sheet's edge, and 0.91% of plate width where both thicknesses are in the line of sight. At the back wall's measured 0.371%/in that lap is 2.5 inches, which is the standard overlap on a bypass shower door. The hangers at x=32.6 and 43.4 both sit right of 31.22, so the SLIDING panel is the right-hand one and the fixed panel is behind it on the left; the handle at 44.01-44.77 is at the slider's far end. RIGHT BOUND: the profile falls steadily to a minimum at x=44.57 and then jumps to a peak of 181 at 45.09. Phase 1 could not tell whether that bright band was the partition's corner or the door's jamb and left it unpainted either way; with the glass mapped it reads as the slider's polished edge. It is left OUT of the polygon — it is the brightest thing in the alcove already, no material paints there, and screening it would only clip it. TOP: the line running across the door plane at y = 8.564 + 0.10716x, which Phase 1 measured and could not place; it is the glazing's head. BOTTOM: the bottom rail's top, y = 97.66 - 0.12x. The two outlines are kept separate because that is what was measured, but the compositor puts both into ONE clip path, so the lap is screened once.
_door_glass_alpha_note: ALPHA 0.22, and ONE value serves a dark wall, a light one and a mid one, because screen is self-limiting: it adds in proportion to (255 - destination), so a near-white panel takes almost nothing while a dark one takes the whole reflection. Predicted lift, plate luminosity about 150 in the glazed field: on a dark slat wall (destination about 95) +19, a 20% lift; on a light Durasein sheet (destination about 205) +6.5, 3.2%. TUNED BY RENDER at 0.28 and 0.18. 0.28 flattened the dark slat panel — the wood lost its richness and the difference between the glazed field and the bare wall above the track read as a wash rather than as glazing. 0.18 held the wood but only just carried the leading edge. 0.22 sits between them. The light case never failed at any of the three, which is the self-limiting property doing its job, so no per-polygon alpha and no brightness weighting were needed.
_door_glass_top_note: THE TOP EDGE IS AT THE TRACK RAIL'S UNDERSIDE, not at the glazing's real head. Measured, the glass runs up to the line y = 8.564 + 0.10716x — the horizontal that Phase 1 found on the door plane and could not place. Carrying the polygon up there was tried and rejected on the render: it puts a hard tonal step straight across open wall at y 11-13, three percent above the rail, and reads as a horizontal seam ruled across the panels rather than as the top of a pane. Anchored instead at y = 15.55 + 0.0935(x - 18.5), the rail's own lower edge, the transition lands where the picture already has a line and reads as the shadow under the track. The cost is that the 3% band of genuinely glazed wall above the rail is not screened; it is mostly covered by the rail and the panel's top-edge treatment, and nothing in it reads as wrong.
